title: Test it a week
hookLine: live the version for seven days: Daniel asks the king's official for a ten-day test of pulse and water
tomorrow: a general was told to wash in a river. why did he storm off?

lines: A FREE TRIAL FOR A LIFE.
cards: A new habit, tried for a week before anyone commits: a free trial for a way of life. Daniel ran one in a palace.
Carried off to Babylon as a young captive, he's chosen to serve the king, and handed the king's own food and wine. Daniel won't take it.
The official in charge is afraid: if you look worse than the others, the king will have my head. So Daniel offers a deal.
"Prove thy servants, I beseech thee, ten days; and let them give us pulse to eat, and water to drink."

teach.b: Pulse is the King James word for plain food grown from seed, like beans. Water instead of wine. Ten days of plain taste, Daniel says, and then look at us and decide.
At the end of the ten days, the text says, their faces looked fairer and fuller than those of all the young men who ate the king's food. Why refuse at all?
The text says "Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king's meat."
Jewish readers see faithfulness to God's law, the dietary laws included, kept far from home, in exile, at a king's table. And notice how he keeps it.

teach.h: NOT A FIGHT: A FAIR TEST.
teach.b: Not with a speech, and not with a fight. With a test: a fixed time, a plain measure, and an honest look at the end. Some Christians keep what they call a Daniel fast, plain foods for a set time, after this story.
That's the teaching in the story: faithfulness is put to a fair trial, and comes through it. A rule of life can be tested the same way.

teach.h: SEVEN DAYS, THEN AN HONEST LOOK.
teach.b: Seven days, lived as written, then an honest look. Not a verdict on you. A test of the version.
If a line doesn't work, the week will show it, and that's what a test is for.

how: Jewish readers see Daniel 1 as keeping God's law, including the dietary laws, in exile; some Christians keep a 'Daniel fast' of plain foods for a set time. A rule of life can be tested the same way: lived as written for a fixed stretch, then reviewed.

games.q: what does “test it a week” mean?
o: a free trial of an app you may subscribe to later
living the version for seven days, then looking honestly
a week of exams at the end of the school term

games.q: the ten-day test: tap the pairs.
p: plain food from seeds: beans, lentils

s: Daniel won the argument with a speech to the king's official
he asked for a test: ten days of pulse and water, then look.
after ten days, the young men on pulse and water looked healthier than the rest
Daniel 1:15: their faces looked fairer and fuller than those who ate the king's food.

games.q: your brother wants to go vegetarian, but his roommate says it'll make him weak. what would Daniel do?
o: propose a fair trial: a set time, then an honest look at the results.
argue it out tonight until the roommate admits he's wrong.
do it in secret so nobody can judge whether it's working.
games.why: Daniel didn't argue; he asked for ten days of pulse and water, and let the result speak.

practice: Pour a glass of water, or hold whatever plain thing is near: a cracker, a piece of fruit. Taste it slowly, nothing added, the way pulse and water might have tasted.
Then read your half-rule once, and tell yourself the start: seven days, beginning now. Stay with the taste for the rest of the time.

wordCard.voice: Test it a week: live the version for seven days, as written, then take an honest look, the way Daniel asked for ten.

carryVoice: The line for the week: test week, a fixed time and an honest look at the end, like Daniel's. Day 1691, and the test begins.
